pos: adv. (before this time; formerly; up to now)
etymology: English here + tofore (before), a compound long naturalized in legal and biblical English. It marks a line between a past manner of things and a change now come.
biblical_def: Heretofore is the KJV's word for the way things have been until now, spoken most often at the moment they stop being so. Moses pleads it as a disqualification: “I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant” (Exo 4:10). Israel is warned by it at the Jordan: “come not near unto it, that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed this way heretofore” (Jos 3:4). Boaz commends Ruth for coming “unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore” (Rut 2:11). And Paul uses it as a warning to the unrepentant: “I write to them which heretofore have sinned… that, if I come again, I will not spare” (2Co 13:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heretofore as in times before the present; formerly; and notes it refers to time past as distinguished from the present.
webster_full: HERETOFORE, adv. In times before the present; formerly.
TOFORE, adv. Before; obsolete except in composition.
FORMERLY, adv. In time past, of longer or shorter duration; heretofore.
scriptures: Exo 4:10
And Moses said unto the LORD, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.
Jos 3:4
Yet there shall be a space between you and it, about two thousand cubits by measure: come not near unto it, that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed this way heretofore.
Rut 2:11

And Boaz answered and said unto her, It hath fully been shewed me, all that thou hast done unto thy mother in law since the death of thine husband: and how thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity, and art come unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore.

I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were present, the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare:
corruption_summary: Joshua 3 tells Israel to follow the ark because they had not passed that way heretofore, and it is the standing pattern for guidance.
corruption_paragraphs: The instruction at the Jordan is one of the plainest statements in Scripture about how God leads. There shall be a space between you and the ark, about two thousand cubits, that ye may know the way by which ye must go — for ye have not passed this way heretofore. Israel is to keep its distance, keep its eyes on the ark, and walk into a country no living Israelite had crossed. Guidance here is not an inward impression or an inference from experience; experience is precisely what is unavailable. It is following the visible token of God's presence, at a reverent distance, into unfamiliar ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's past is not his map. Moses answers the burning bush with his history — I am not eloquent, neither heretofore — and God answers with a question about who made the mouth. The reflex is common and looks like humility: I have never been able to do this, therefore God cannot be calling me to it. Exodus 4 treats it as unbelief, and Exodus 4:14 records that the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses over it. The word heretofore describes what God is about to change.
roots_summary: Hebrew tmol shilshom, literally yesterday and the day before — the idiom the KJV renders heretofore; Greek proamartano (G4258), to have sinned before.
roots_lines: Hebrew tmol shilshom — yesterday and third day, i.e. formerly; Exodus 4:10, Joshua 3:4.
Hebrew ethmol (H865) — yesterday, before; Ruth 2:11, 2 Samuel 15:20.
Greek proamartano (G4258) — to sin beforehand; 2 Corinthians 12:21, 13:2 only.
Hebrew aron (H727) — ark; Joshua 3:3, 3:4.
Hebrew rachaq (H7368) — to be far, keep distance; Joshua 3:4, Proverbs 22:5.
usage: “Ye have not passed this way heretofore” — the reason to follow the ark.
“I am not eloquent, neither heretofore” — Moses' history offered as a refusal.
“Them which heretofore have sinned” — Paul's warning to Corinth.

pos: adv. (in whatever manner; nevertheless; at all events)
etymology: English how + soever, an intensifying compound of so + ever. In the KJV it usually carries the force of in any case or be that as it may.
biblical_def: The old man of Gibeah presses hospitality with it: “Peace be with thee; howsoever let all thy wants lie upon me; only lodge not in the street” (Jdg 19:20). Ahimaaz uses it twice to overrule Joab's refusal: “But howsoever, let me, I pray thee, also run after Cushi” (2Sa 18:22), and again, “But howsoever, said he, let me run” (2Sa 18:23). And the LORD uses it of a nation that would not learn: “Surely thou wilt fear me, thou wilt receive instruction; so their dwelling should not be cut off, howsoever I punished them: but they rose early, and corrupted all their doings” (Zep 3:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines howsoever as in what manner soever; although; however; and notes that it is now generally written however.
webster_full: HOWSOEVER, adv. In what manner soever.
HOWSOEVER, adv. Although; however. This word is now generally written however.
SOEVER, A word compounded of so and ever, used to extend or render indefinite the signification of who, what, where, how.
scriptures: And the old man said, Peace be with thee; howsoever let all thy wants lie upon me; only lodge not in the street.
Then said Ahimaaz the son of Zadok yet again to Joab, But howsoever, let me, I pray thee, also run after Cushi. And Joab said, Wherefore wilt thou run, my son, seeing that thou hast no tidings ready?
But howsoever, said he, let me run. And he said unto him, Run. Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi.
Zep 3:7
I said, Surely thou wilt fear me, thou wilt receive instruction; so their dwelling should not be cut off, howsoever I punished them: but they rose early, and corrupted all their doings.
corruption_summary: Zephaniah 3:7 records a people punished repeatedly and unchanged by it, which Scripture treats as the deepest kind of hardness.
corruption_paragraphs: Zephaniah 3:7 is God reviewing a long and fruitless discipline. He had said surely thou wilt fear me, thou wilt receive instruction; the chastisements came, howsoever He punished them — and they rose early and corrupted all their doings. Amos 4 says the same thing five times over with a refrain: I have given you cleanness of teeth, I have withholden the rain, I have smitten you with blasting and mildew — yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD. Affliction is not automatically sanctifying. It softens or it hardens, and which it does is a matter of the heart that receives it.

The corruption to name is the sentimental doctrine that suffering makes people better, which is a half-truth that leaves the sufferer with no reason to repent. Hebrews 12 gives the true account: chastening yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. The exercise is the condition. Pharaoh was hardened under ten plagues, the men in Revelation 16 gnaw their tongues for pain and blaspheme the God of heaven and repent not of their deeds, and Zephaniah's Jerusalem rose early to corrupt her doings. The right use of an affliction is not endurance but return.
roots_summary: Hebrew aken / ak, surely, nevertheless; yasar (H3256), to instruct by chastening; musar (H4148), instruction, correction.
roots_lines: Hebrew ak (H389) — surely, only, nevertheless; Zephaniah 3:7, Psalm 73:1.
Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to chasten, instruct; Zephaniah 3:7, Proverbs 19:18.
Hebrew musar (H4148) — instruction, discipline; Zephaniah 3:7, Proverbs 1:8.
Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to corrupt, destroy; Zephaniah 3:7, Genesis 6:12.
Hebrew shakam (H7925) — to rise early; Zephaniah 3:7, Jeremiah 7:13.
usage: “Howsoever let all thy wants lie upon me” — hospitality pressed on a stranger.
“But howsoever, said he, let me run” — Ahimaaz overruling Joab.
“Howsoever I punished them” — discipline that did not reach the heart.

pos: adv. (at whatever time; as often as; whenever)
etymology: English when + soever. The compound leaves the time open — it is the language of an occasion that will recur and a duty that stands whenever it does.
biblical_def: Jacob's husbandry runs by it: “whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle” (Gen 30:41). Paul plans by it: “Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you… and to be brought on my way thitherward by you” (Rom 15:24). And Christ turns it into a standing charge concerning the poor: “ye have the poor with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good: but me ye have not always” (Mar 14:7), which Matthew records as “ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always” (Mat 26:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines whensoever as at what time soever; at whatever time.
webster_full: WHENSOEVER, adv. At what time soever; at whatever time.
WHENEVER, adv. At whatever time.
SOEVER, A word used to render the sense indefinite, and generally united with who, what, where, when, how.
scriptures: And it came to pass, whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods.
Mar 14:7
For ye have the poor with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good: but me ye have not always.
For ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always.
Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I trust to see you in my journey, and to be brought on my way thitherward by you, if first I be somewhat filled with your company.
corruption_summary: Christ's word about the poor is a charge to do them good whensoever we will, not a shrug at poverty as permanent and therefore unaddressable.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 14:7 is among the most misquoted sentences in the Gospels. Christ is defending a woman whose costly ointment the disciples called waste, and He says two things: the poor ye have with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good. The second clause is the commandment, and it is usually dropped. He is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11 — the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy. The permanence of poverty is stated in Scripture as the ground of ongoing generosity, never as an excuse to stop.

The corruption to name runs in two directions and the verse is misused by both. On one side it is quoted to dismiss the care of the poor as futile, which is precisely the inversion of Deuteronomy 15:11. On the other side it is treated as an embarrassment to be explained away by those who make material relief the substance of the gospel, when Christ's point was that His own person outranked even a true and commanded duty in that hour. The church is to hold both: worship of Christ is never waste, and open-handedness to the poor is commanded whensoever we will.
roots_summary: Greek hotan (G3752), whenever, as often as; Greek ptochos (G4434), the destitute poor; Hebrew ebyon (H34), the needy.
roots_lines: Greek hotan (G3752) — whensoever, whenever; Mark 14:7, Matthew 6:2.
Greek ptochos (G4434) — poor, beggarly, destitute; Mark 14:7, Luke 4:18.
Hebrew ebyon (H34) — needy, poor; Deuteronomy 15:11, Psalm 72:4.
Greek eupoieo (G2109) — to do good; Mark 14:7, Hebrews 13:16.
Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to bind, be stronger; Genesis 30:41, 30:42.
usage: “Whensoever ye will ye may do them good” — the half of the verse usually dropped.
“Whensoever I take my journey into Spain” — Paul's westward plan.
“Whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive” — Jacob at Laban's flocks.

pos: adv. (toward that place; in that direction)
etymology: Old English thider, to that place, + -weard, in the direction of. The word describes a face set toward a destination rather than an arrival at one.
biblical_def: The Danites turn aside to Micah's house: “And they turned thitherward, and came to the house of the young man the Levite” (Jdg 18:15). Paul hopes for an escort westward: “to be brought on my way thitherward by you” (Rom 15:24). And Jeremiah uses it for the return from exile, in one of the most moving pictures of repentance in the prophets: “They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten” (Jer 50:5) — a people “going and weeping: they shall go, and seek the LORD their God” (Jer 50:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thitherward as toward that place, and thither as to that place, in opposition to hither, or to this place.
webster_full: THITHERWARD, adv. Toward that place.
THITHER, adv. To that place, in opposition to hither, or to this place.
WARD, A termination signifying direction, or turning toward; as in homeward, heavenward.
scriptures: And they turned thitherward, and came to the house of the young man the Levite, even unto the house of Micah, and saluted him.
Jer 50:4
In those days, and in that time, saith the LORD, the children of Israel shall come, they and the children of Judah together, going and weeping: they shall go, and seek the LORD their God.
Jer 50:5
They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten.
Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I trust to see you in my journey, and to be brought on my way thitherward by you, if first I be somewhat filled with your company.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah's returning exiles ask the way to Zion with their faces already turned toward it, which is repentance described as direction.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 50:4-5 gives repentance in three movements and every one of them matters. They come going and weeping — there is sorrow, and it is not the end but the beginning. They ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward — the direction is settled before the route is known, which is the difference between genuine turning and mere regret. And they say, come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten — the goal is not relief from exile but union with God on covenant terms. Paul's account in 2 Corinthians 7 matches it: godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of.

The corruption to name is sorrow mistaken for repentance. Esau found no place of repentance though he sought it carefully with tears; Judas repented himself in the sense of remorse and went and hanged himself; Saul said I have sinned more than once and never turned. Tears are in Jeremiah's picture, but so is a face. What distinguishes the exiles is that they are pointed somewhere — away from Babylon, toward Zion, into a covenant — and they are asking for the road. The modern therapeutic substitute stops at the feeling and calls the discomfort itself a kind of penance. Scripture asks which way the face is turned.
roots_summary: Hebrew hennah (H2008), hither, thither; panim (H6440), face, presence; derek (H1870), way, road, manner of life.
roots_lines: Hebrew hennah (H2008) — hither, thither; Jeremiah 50:5, Genesis 15:16.
Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, presence, countenance; Jeremiah 50:5, Psalm 27:8.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — way, road, manner; Jeremiah 50:5, Psalm 1:6.
Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, return, repent; Jeremiah 50:4, Hosea 14:1.
Greek propempo (G4311) — to send forward, bring on the way; Romans 15:24, Titus 3:13.
usage: “With their faces thitherward” — repentance described as a direction.
“To be brought on my way thitherward by you” — Paul asking Rome for an escort.
“And they turned thitherward” — the Danites at Micah's door.

pos: adv. (upon that; in consequence of that; immediately after)
etymology: English there + upon. The KJV uses it both spatially — resting upon that thing — and consequentially, of what follows from a foundation already laid.
biblical_def: Thereupon is a builder's word. Of the tabernacle: “the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is thereupon” (Exo 31:7). Of the church: “as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon” (1Co 3:10), a warning grounded in the fact that “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11), and enforced by the day of testing: “If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward” (1Co 3:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thereupon as upon that or it; in consequence of that; and immediately.
webster_full: THEREUPON, adv. Upon that or it.
THEREUPON, adv. In consequence of that.
THEREUPON, adv. Immediately; at once; without delay.
scriptures: Exo 31:7
The tabernacle of the congregation, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is thereupon, and all the furniture of the tabernacle,
According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward.
corruption_summary: The foundation is fixed and unrepeatable, and every minister's liberty is confined to how he builds on it.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 3 draws a line the church keeps needing. The foundation is laid, once, and it is Jesus Christ; no man can lay another, and the attempt is not innovation but destruction. What remains open is the building — gold, silver, precious stones, or wood, hay, stubble — and the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire. Paul's warning is addressed to builders, that is, to preachers and teachers, and it does not threaten their salvation but their work: he shall suffer loss, but he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire. Ministry is examined, and much of it burns.

The corruption to name is the ambition to lay a new foundation, which is what every serious doctrinal novelty amounts to. It rarely announces itself that way; it comes as a fresh angle, a recovered emphasis, a necessary adjustment to the age. The test Paul gives is objective — is the thing being built resting on Christ as He is set forth in the apostolic gospel, or is it resting on something else and using His name? The second half of the warning is just as needful for the orthodox: a right foundation does not sanctify shoddy work built upon it, and stubble laid on Christ is still stubble.
roots_summary: Greek epoikodomeo (G2026), to build upon; themelios (G2310), foundation; Hebrew al (H5921), upon, over.
roots_lines: Greek epoikodomeo (G2026) — to build upon; 1 Corinthians 3:10, 3:12, Ephesians 2:20.
Greek themelios (G2310) — foundation; 1 Corinthians 3:11, Hebrews 6:1.
Greek architekton (G753) — masterbuilder; 1 Corinthians 3:10 only.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to try, test, prove; 1 Corinthians 3:13, 1 Thessalonians 2:4.
Hebrew kapporeth (H3727) — mercy seat; Exodus 31:7, 25:17.
usage: “Let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon” — the warning to builders.
“If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon” — the day will show.
“The mercy seat that is thereupon” — the ark and its covering.

etymology: English oft + times, an old adverbial compound. It marks a settled pattern rather than a single occurrence — something that has happened again and again.
biblical_def: The father of the demoniac boy uses it to describe years of torment: “he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water” (Mat 17:15), and to Christ, “ofttimes it hath cast him into the fire, and into the waters, to destroy him: but if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us” (Mar 9:22). To that half-faith Christ replies, and the father answers with the prayer of the whole church: “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” (Mar 9:24). John uses the word of a settled habit of prayer: “Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place: for Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples” (Joh 18:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ofttimes and oftentimes as frequently, often, many times, and oft as an adverb signifying often or frequently.
webster_full: OFTTIMES, adv. Frequently; often; many times.
OFT, adv. Often; frequently; not rarely. It is used chiefly in poetry.
OFTEN, adv. Frequently; many times; not seldom.
scriptures: Lord, have mercy on my son: for he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water.
Mar 9:22
And ofttimes it hath cast him into the fire, and into the waters, to destroy him: but if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us.
Mar 9:24
And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
Joh 18:2
And Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place: for Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples.
corruption_summary: A father with a doubting if thou canst is not turned away, and his cry becomes the model prayer of imperfect faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 9 is the passage every honest believer needs. The father has watched his son thrown into fire and water for years, has already been failed by the disciples, and can only manage if thou canst do any thing. Christ presses the if back on him, and the man breaks: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. He confesses faith and unbelief in one breath, and the child is healed. This is not a commendation of weak faith as though weakness were a virtue; it is a demonstration that the object of faith saves, and not the strength of the grip. A trembling hand on Christ holds a Christ who does not tremble.

The corruption to name is the doctrine, in its charismatic and its secular forms alike, that outcomes are governed by the intensity of one's believing — that the healing failed because the faith was insufficient. Mark 9 destroys it: the faith on display is explicitly insufficient and the boy is delivered anyway. The other side of the ditch is just as real, the settled unbelief that never cries out at all. The father does the one thing required of him. He brings what faith he has, tells the truth about its size, and asks Christ to supply the rest — which is what the Reformed doctrine of faith as a gift has always meant.
roots_summary: Greek pollakis (G4178), often, many times; apistia (G570), unbelief; boetheo (G997), to run to help.
roots_lines: Greek pollakis (G4178) — often, ofttimes; Matthew 17:15, Mark 9:22, 2 Corinthians 11:23.
Greek apistia (G570) — unbelief; Mark 9:24, Romans 4:20, Hebrews 3:12.
Greek boetheo (G997) — to help, succour; Mark 9:22, 9:24, Hebrews 2:18.
Greek splanchnizomai (G4697) — to be moved with compassion; Mark 9:22, Matthew 9:36.
Greek selniazomai (G4583) — to be lunatick, moonstruck; Matthew 17:15, 4:24.
usage: “Ofttimes he falleth into the fire” — years of torment in one word.
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” — the prayer of honest faith.
“Jesus ofttimes resorted thither” — a habit of prayer Judas could count on.

pos: n. and adv. (last night; the night just past)
etymology: Old English geostran, yesterday, + niht. The word survives in Scripture chiefly in Genesis, where God repeatedly acts in the night that has just gone by.
biblical_def: Yesternight marks a night God has already used. Laban pursues Jacob with a threat and a confession in the same sentence: “It is in the power of my hand to do you hurt: but the God of your father spake unto me yesternight, saying, Take thou heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad” (Gen 31:29) — Moses records the dream itself in Gen 31:24. Jacob throws it back at him: “God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked thee yesternight” (Gen 31:42). The word also stands over the darkest night in Lot's family: “Behold, I lay yesternight with my father” (Gen 19:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines yesternight as on the night last past, and yester as an adjective denoting the last past, applied to a portion of time.
webster_full: YESTERNIGHT, n. The last night.
YESTERNIGHT, adv. On the last night.
YESTER, a. Last; last past; next before the present; as yesterday, yesternight.
scriptures: And it came to pass on the morrow, that the firstborn said unto the younger, Behold, I lay yesternight with my father: let us make him drink wine this night also; and go thou in, and lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.
And God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night, and said unto him, Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad.
It is in the power of my hand to do you hurt: but the God of your father spake unto me yesternight, saying, Take thou heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad.

Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty. God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked thee yesternight.
corruption_summary: Laban had the power and the intention to destroy Jacob, and was stopped in a dream he did not ask for and could not refuse.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 31 shows providence working through a man who has no interest in serving it. Laban has pursued Jacob seven days with armed kinsmen, and by his own account it was in the power of his hand to do him hurt. What stopped him was a dream. God came to Laban the Syrian — not a covenant man, not a worshipper, a schemer who kept household idols — and restrained him with a word he did not seek. Jacob sees it plainly: God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked thee yesternight. The protection of God's people frequently runs through the restrained malice of their enemies, and they hear about it afterward.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's hardest work on our behalf is usually invisible to us at the time. Jacob spent that night not knowing that his father-in-law had been warned; he had spent twenty years not knowing how much had been kept off him. Psalm 121 states the doctrine flatly — he that keepeth thee will not slumber; the LORD is thy keeper. The believer's account of his own life will always be incomplete on this side, because the dangers averted leave no record. Laban's dream is in Scripture so we know the category exists.
roots_summary: Hebrew emesh (H570), yesternight, last night; chalom (H2472), dream; yakach (H3198), to reprove, rebuke.
roots_lines: Hebrew emesh (H570) — yesternight, last evening; Genesis 19:34, 31:29, 31:42, 2 Kings 9:26.
Hebrew chalom (H2472) — dream; Genesis 31:24, 20:3, 37:5.
Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, rebuke, judge; Genesis 31:42, Proverbs 3:12.
Hebrew oni (H6040) — affliction; Genesis 31:42, Exodus 3:7.
Hebrew pachad (H6343) — fear, dread; Genesis 31:42, 31:53.
usage: “The God of your father spake unto me yesternight” — Laban restrained in a dream.
“God hath seen mine affliction… and rebuked thee yesternight” — Jacob's answer.
“I lay yesternight with my father” — the ruin of Lot's house.

pos: adv. (with speed; at a quick pace; fast)
etymology: English a- (on) + pace, from Latin passus, a step. It describes motion at speed, whether of a runner bringing news or of an army in flight.
biblical_def: The watchman on the wall reports a runner: “If he be alone, there is tidings in his mouth. And he came apace, and drew near” (2Sa 18:25), and recognizes him a moment later — “the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok. And the king said, He is a good man, and cometh with good tidings” (2Sa 18:27). The psalmist uses it of routed enemies: “Kings of armies did flee apace: and she that tarried at home divided the spoil” (Psa 68:12). Jeremiah uses it of Egypt broken at Carchemish: “their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: for fear was round about, saith the LORD” (Jer 46:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apace as with a quick pace; quick; fast; speedily; with haste; hastily.
webster_full: APACE, adv. With a quick pace; quick; fast; speedily; with haste; hastily; applied to things in motion.
PACE, n. A step; the space between the two feet in walking, estimated at two feet and a half.
HASTE, n. Celerity of motion; speed; swiftness; dispatch; expedition.
scriptures: And the watchman cried, and told the king. And the king said, If he be alone, there is tidings in his mouth. And he came apace, and drew near.
And the watchman said, Me thinketh the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok. And the king said, He is a good man, and cometh with good tidings.
Kings of armies did flee apace: and she that tarried at home divided the spoil.
Jer 46:5
Wherefore have I seen them dismayed and turned away back? and their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: for fear was round about, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: David watched a good man run fast with good tidings and got the worst news of his life, which is Scripture's standing warning against reading providence by appearances.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Samuel 18 is painful and instructive. David sits between the gates; the watchman sees a lone runner coming apace; the king reasons that a solitary runner carries news rather than a rout, and when the man is identified as Ahimaaz he says, he is a good man, and cometh with good tidings. The reasoning is sound and the conclusion is wrong. Ahimaaz brings a victory report and cannot bring himself to say the rest, and it is Cushi who tells the father that Absalom is dead. Every inference David drew from what he could see was reasonable, and none of it prepared him for what the day held.

The corruption to name is the reading of providence as a running commentary on God's favour, which Scripture nowhere authorizes. Ecclesiastes 9 says no man knoweth either love or hatred by all that is before them; Job's friends were rebuked for exactly this method; and Christ refused it directly concerning the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled and the eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell. The believer reads God's heart in the Scriptures and at the cross, not off the surface of events. What he owes to events is trust and obedience, not interpretation.

pos: adv. (on the contrary; in the opposite manner; conversely)
etymology: English contrary, from Latin contrarius, opposite, + -wise, in the manner of. Paul and Peter use it to pivot hard from what men expect to what God commands.
biblical_def: Contrariwise turns a sentence around. Paul on the repentant offender: “So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2Co 2:7). Paul on the apostolic division of labour: “But contrariwise, when they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter” (Gal 2:7), because “he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles” (Gal 2:8). And Peter on the Christian answer to injury: “Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing” (1Pe 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contrariwise as on the contrary; oppositely; on the other hand.
webster_full: CONTRARIWISE, adv. On the contrary; oppositely; on the other hand.
CONTRARY, a. Opposite; adverse; moving against or in an opposite direction.
CONVERSELY, adv. With inversion of order; in a contrary order; reciprocally.
scriptures: So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
Gal 2:7
But contrariwise, when they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter;
Gal 2:8
(For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles:)
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
corruption_summary: Second Corinthians 2 requires a church that has rightly disciplined a man to forgive and comfort him, and names the danger of refusing.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul had commanded the Corinthians to put the offender out. Now he commands them, contrariwise, to forgive him and comfort him, and to confirm their love toward him, lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow — adding that Satan gains an advantage where this is neglected, for we are not ignorant of his devices. Discipline in the New Testament is medicinal from beginning to end. Its aim is the restoration of the offender and the purity of the church, and a congregation that can excommunicate but cannot restore has kept half a commandment.

The corruption to name is at both extremes, and the church usually falls into whichever one it is not currently worried about. On one side is the refusal to discipline at all — the congregation that mistakes tolerance of scandal for love, which 1 Corinthians 5 forbids in the plainest terms. On the other is the discipline that never ends, where repentance is received with suspicion and the restored man carries his old sin as a permanent status. Peter's contrariwise blessing is the same instinct applied to enemies outside: the Christian's reflex under injury is neither retaliation nor silence, but blessing, because he was himself called to inherit one.

pos: conj. (during the time that; while; as long as)
etymology: Middle English whiles with an added -t, from Old English hwil, a space of time. In the KJV it marks a window that is open and will not stay so.
biblical_def: Whilst names a limited opportunity. Joash demands justice on Baal's behalf within a set time: “he that will plead for him, let him be put to death whilst it is yet morning: if he be a god, let him plead for himself” (Jdg 6:31). Nehemiah refuses to leave the wall: “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?” (Neh 6:3). Bildad describes the swiftness of the hypocrite's end: “Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb” (Job 8:12). And David prays, “Let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape” (Psa 141:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines whilst as during the time that, and while as a noun meaning a space of time, or a time short or long.
webster_full: WHILST, adv. During the time that; as long as; whilst is now less used than while.
WHILE, n. Time; space of time, or continued duration; as, one shall be taken and another left; a long while.
WHILE, adv. During the time that; as long as.
scriptures: Jdg 6:31

And Joash said unto all that stood against him, Will ye plead for Baal? will ye save him? he that will plead for him, let him be put to death whilst it is yet morning: if he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar.
Neh 6:3
And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?
Job 8:12
Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb.
Let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape.
corruption_summary: Nehemiah refused four invitations to a conference in the plain of Ono because coming down from the wall was the point of the invitation.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 6 is a short course in resisting distraction dressed as reasonableness. Sanballat and Geshem propose a meeting; the location is neutral, the tone is collegial, and Nehemiah discerns that they thought to do him mischief. His answer contains no argument and no negotiation: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down; why should the work cease, whilst I leave it? They sent four times after this sort, and he answered them after the same manner. The wall was finished in fifty-two days, and the enemies perceived that the work was wrought of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a good answer to a bad request does not need to be clever, only steady and repeated. Note also what Nehemiah does not do: he does not denounce them, does not litigate the accusation that he means to be king, does not go down to explain himself. Joash in Judges 6 shows the other side of the same sobriety — if Baal is a god, let him plead for himself, whilst it is yet morning. Both men decline to spend their strength on a contest that God will settle without them.
